title: Politics in India: Politics of Planned Development

learn.hook: A hill rich in iron ore can mean a steel plant and thousands of jobs, or forests lost and villages displaced. Which path should a state choose, and who decides?
points: Development decisions are political: they involve choices between different groups with competing interests, and so they are contested in a democracy.
No single decision suits everyone. What benefits one group, such as industry or urban consumers, may harm another, such as tribal communities or farmers.
Example: Odisha has some of the largest untapped reserves of iron ore in India. The state government signed agreements with steel companies to set up plants, hoping for investment and jobs.

Tribal communities feared displacement from their land and loss of livelihood; environmentalists warned of pollution and damage to forests; others argued that industry was essential for the state's growth.
Such debates show that the question of development is not just technical but also about values and whose interests count.

example.q: List the groups with competing views on iron-ore mining and steel plants in Odisha.
steps: State government and industry: want investment, jobs and growth.
Tribal communities: fear displacement and loss of livelihood.
Environmentalists: fear pollution and destruction of forests.
example.answer: Government and industry; tribal communities; environmentalists

learn.reallife: Debates over new airports, expressways, dams or mines in your own state follow the same pattern: jobs and growth on one side, displacement and environment on the other.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

learn.hook: In 1947 India had two famous models to copy: the American and the Soviet. It chose neither completely.
points: In the 1940s and 1950s, development was often understood as becoming 'modern', which meant becoming like the industrialised countries of the West. Modernisation was linked with growth, industrialisation and material progress.
There were two models of modern development: the liberal-capitalist model, as in the USA and much of Europe, and the socialist model, as in the USSR.
Many Indian leaders, including Nehru, were impressed by the Soviet model of rapid industrialisation, but India did not copy either model fully.

Left and right: the 'left' favoured pro-poor policies and a strong role for the state to reduce inequality; the 'right' favoured free competition and a market economy, with less government interference.
India's leaders agreed that development could not be left to private actors alone; the state had to play a key role. They disagreed about how much.

example.q: Classify these views as left or right: (a) the state should own key industries to reduce inequality (b) markets should decide prices with minimal government role.
steps: (a) Strong state role for the poor: left.
(b) Free market and less interference: right.

learn.reallife: Debates today about privatising public sector banks or Air India are modern versions of the old left-right debate on the state's role.

games.title: Match the model
pairs: Strong state role for the poor

quiz.explain: Modernisation meant industrial growth on the Western pattern.

quiz.explain: The US and Soviet models were the two main options.

quiz.q: Which is a 'left' position on development?

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Misses the appeal of rapid industrialisation

quiz.q: Assertion (A): India's leaders agreed that the state should play no role in development. Reason (R): Indian leaders debated how large the state's role should be.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: they agreed the state had a key role. R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'In 1947, how did India decide what kind of development to have?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Development meant becoming modern; there were capitalist and socialist models, left and right debated the state's role, and India mixed both!
teach.nudge: Good. What were the two models, and what did left and right want?

topics.title: Planning: the Bombay Plan, the Planning Commission and NITI Aayog

learn.hook: Surprisingly, one of the strongest calls for state planning in India came from big industrialists, in 1944.
points: There was a broad consensus that India should plan its development. In 1944, a group of big industrialists drafted a joint proposal for a planned economy, called the Bombay Plan. It wanted the state to take major initiatives in industrial and other economic investments.

The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by a simple resolution of the Government of India. It had an advisory role, and the Prime Minister was its chairperson. It was not set up by the Constitution or by a separate law.

A Five Year Plan is a document in which the government sets out its plan for income and expenditure over five years. Planning lets the government focus on the larger picture and make long-term interventions in the economy.
The Planning Commission was replaced by the NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) in 2015.

example.q: Was the Planning Commission a constitutional body?
steps: It was set up in March 1950.
It was created by a simple resolution of the Government of India.
So it was neither constitutional nor statutory; it was advisory.
example.answer: No; it was set up by a government resolution and was advisory

learn.reallife: NITI Aayog now publishes indices like the SDG India Index and works with states, instead of drawing up Five Year Plans.

topics.title: The First and Second Five Year Plans

learn.hook: The First Plan said: feed the nation first. The Second Plan said: build steel, power and machines fast. Two plans, two philosophies.
points: The First Five Year Plan (1951-56) focused on the agrarian sector, including investment in dams and irrigation. Agriculture had been badly hit by Partition, and land reforms were seen as key to development.
K.N. Raj, a young economist who helped draft the First Plan, argued that India should 'hasten slowly' for the first two decades.
The Second Five Year Plan (1956-61) stressed heavy industrialisation, and was drafted under the leadership of P.C. Mahalanobis.
To protect domestic industries, the government imposed substantial tariffs on imports. Public sector industries were set up in steel, power and machinery.
Exam tip: First Plan = agriculture, dams, irrigation, K.N. Raj; Second Plan = heavy industry, P.C. Mahalanobis.

example.q: Compare the First and Second Five Year Plans in a table.
steps: First Plan (1951-56): agriculture, dams, irrigation; K.N. Raj ('hasten slowly').
Second Plan (1956-61): rapid heavy industrialisation; P.C. Mahalanobis; tariffs to protect domestic industry.
example.answer: First: agriculture-led (K.N. Raj); Second: heavy industry-led (Mahalanobis)

learn.reallife: The Bhakra Nangal dam, which irrigates fields in Punjab and Haryana, and the Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur steel plants are symbols of the first two Plans.

quiz.q: The main focus of the First Five Year Plan was:
quiz.explain: Agriculture had been hit by Partition and needed investment.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Second Plan

quiz.q: Who argued that India should 'hasten slowly' in the first two decades?
quiz.explain: K.N. Raj, a young economist, made this argument.
quiz.mistake: Credits Mahalanobis, linked to the Second Plan

quiz.q: The Second Five Year Plan was drafted under the leadership of:
quiz.explain: Mahalanobis led the Second Plan's industrial strategy.
quiz.mistake: Confuses him with K.N. Raj

quiz.q: The Second Five Year Plan stressed:
quiz.explain: It emphasised rapid growth of heavy industry.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the First Plan

quiz.q: The period of the First Five Year Plan was:
quiz.explain: The First Plan ran from 1951 to 1956.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the plan periods

quiz.q: How did the government protect domestic industries under the Second Plan?
options: By removing all taxes on imports
By imposing substantial tariffs on imports
quiz.explain: Tariffs shielded domestic industry from foreign competition.
quiz.mistake: Picks an open-economy measure

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The First Plan gave priority to agriculture. Reason (R): Agriculture had been badly affected by Partition.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R explains the priority.
quiz.mistake: Misses why agriculture came first

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The Second Plan focused mainly on agriculture and irrigation. Reason (R): P.C. Mahalanobis led the drafting of the Second Plan.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: it focused on heavy industry. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the focus of the two plans

teach.praise: Hooray! The First Plan focused on farms, dams and irrigation (K.N. Raj), and the Second on heavy industry (Mahalanobis)!

topics.title: Public sector, import substitution and the mixed economy

learn.hook: India's early steel plants were built by the state, while textile mills and shops stayed private. That mix had a name: the mixed economy.
points: The public sector (industries owned by the government) was given a leading role in key areas such as steel, mining, power and heavy machinery.
Import substitution meant producing at home the goods that were earlier imported, protected by tariffs and controls on imports.
India adopted a mixed economy: both the public sector and the private sector existed, but the state played a major role in planning and in key industries.

Critics from the right said the state controlled too much, creating a licence-permit system and inefficiency. Critics from the left said the private sector and the rich gained too much, and the poor too little.
Exercise tip: compare the First and Second Plans, and explain the two models of development and why India chose a mixed path.

example.q: Explain the term 'mixed economy' with an Indian example.
steps: A mixed economy has both public and private sectors.
Example: the state built steel plants (public sector), while private firms ran textile mills and consumer goods industries.
The state also planned and regulated the economy.
example.answer: An economy with both public and private sectors, with a key planning role for the state

learn.reallife: Companies like SAIL (steel), BHEL (heavy electricals) and ONGC (oil) are public sector firms whose origins lie in the planning era.

Both public and private sectors exist

quiz.mistake: Assigns a left criticism to the right

options: The private sector and the rich gained too much while the poor gained little
quiz.explain: The left said benefits went disproportionately to the rich.
quiz.mistake: Assigns a right criticism to the left

quiz.q: Why were tariffs imposed on imports during the planning era?

quiz.mistake: Misreads the purpose of tariffs

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Misunderstands 'mixed'

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: India kept a private sector too. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Equates a strong public sector with full socialism

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Did the government own everything in India's planned economy?'
teach.praise: Chirp! India had a mixed economy: a strong public sector in key industries plus a private sector, with import substitution, and critics on both left and right!
teach.nudge: Good. What does 'mixed economy' mean, and what is import substitution?
